scenes.title: Core Problem and Operational Context
scenes.scene_goal: Introduce Solara Energy operational domain challenge and agent diversity.
scenes.voiceover_narration: We introduced Solara Energy and looked at how agents can take a goal like monitoring site performance and turn it into a sequence of real actions, querying data, comparing outputs, flagging anomalies, and generating reports. But not all agents work the same way. There are different types, built on different architectures, designed for different kinds of problems. And understanding those differences is what allows you to match the right agent to the right job.

scenes.title: Four Pillars of AI Agent Architecture
scenes.scene_goal: Detailed structural breakdown of the 4 core pillars inside an AI agent.
scenes.voiceover_narration: Let's start with what's inside. Every AI agent, regardless of type, is built from the same fundamental components. There's the perception layer. This is how the agent receives information from the world around it. At Solara, that might mean reading an incoming data feed from a solar installation, receiving a user query, or picking up a trigger from a monitoring system. There's the memory layer. As we covered in the last topic, agents hold short-term context within a task and can access long-term memory from external storage. This is what allows an agent to reason across multiple steps without losing track of where it is. There's the reasoning engine, the LLM, which interprets what the agent has perceived, decides what to do next, and determines which tools to use. And there's the action layer. This is where the agent does something in the world, runs a query, calls an API, writes a file, sends an alert.

scenes.title: Continuous Agent-Environment Feedback Loop
scenes.scene_goal: Explain the dynamic feedback loop connecting agent state to external environment.
scenes.voiceover_narration: These four components work together in a continuous loop. The agent perceives, reasons, acts, then perceives again based on the result of that action. That loop is what we call agent-environment interaction. And it's worth understanding because it's what separates an agent from a static tool. A static tool waits to be asked. An agent operates within an environment. It observes what's happening, decides what action is appropriate, and executes. Then it checks the result and decides what comes next. At Solara, an agent monitoring grid performance isn't just waiting for someone to run a report. It's watching. When output at a site drops below threshold, it observes the deviation, decides the appropriate response, which might be querying historical data, cross-referencing weather records, or escalating to a human operator, and takes that action. The environment shapes the agent. The agent shapes the environment.

scenes.title: Perceive-Reason-Act (PRA) Execution Cycle
scenes.scene_goal: Deep walkthrough of the micro-execution PRA cycle driving every decision.
scenes.voiceover_narration: That bi-directional relationship is what makes agents useful in dynamic, real-world data contexts. Let's slow that loop down and look at each stage. Perception is input. The agent receives information, a data reading, a user request, a tool result, and error message. It takes that in and adds it to its working context. Reasoning is interpretation and planning. The agent's LLM process is what it's received, considers its goal, reviews what it's already done, and decides what action to take next. This is where the intelligence lives. Action is execution. The agent calls a tool, writes an output, sends a message or updates a record. Something changes in the world as a result. Then the cycle begins again. The result of the action becomes new perception. The agent reasons about what that result means. For Solaris Equipment Health Monitoring Agent, this cycle might run dozens of times in a single task. Querying data, evaluating results, deciding what to check next, generating a finding before it produces a final output. Now let's talk about the three main types.

scenes.title: Architecture Types 1 & 2: Reactive vs Goal-Based Agents
scenes.scene_goal: Contrast reflex-based condition-action rules against future-state goal planning.
scenes.voiceover_narration: agents because not every problem needs the same architecture. The first type is the reactive agent. A reactive agent responds to its current input using predefined rules. It has no memory of what happened before, no ability to plan ahead. It simply observes a condition and responds. Think of a simple alert agent at Solara. If output at site 12 drops below 8% of a baseline, send a notification. That's a reactive agent. Fast, predictable, easy to build, but limited. It can't investigate why the drop happened or determine whether the alert is actually worth sending. The second type is the goal-based agent. A goal-based agent reasons about actions in terms of whether they move it closer to a defined outcome. It plans, it evaluates options, it chooses the path most likely to achieve the goal. Solara's site performance investigation agent works this way. Its goal is to determine why site 47 underperformed last Tuesday. It doesn't follow a fixed script. It decides what data to pull based on what it finds, adjusting its approach as results come in.

scenes.title: Architecture Type 3: Utility-Based Agents & Workflow
scenes.scene_goal: Multi-objective utility optimization and closed-loop workflow with human handoff.
scenes.voiceover_narration: The third type is the utility-based agent. A utility-based agent goes further than goal-based reasoning. It doesn't just ask, will this action achieve the goal. It asks, which available action achieves the goal most efficiently, at the lowest cost and with the highest confidence. At Solara, a utility-based agent managing report generation across hundreds of sites needs to make trade-off decisions constantly. Do I generate a full diagnostic report or a summary? Do I escalate this anomaly or log it for review? It evaluates options against a utility function and picks the best one. Let's zoom out and look at how these components and concepts come together in a complete agent workflow. A goal arrives. The agent perceives it, adds it to context and begins reasoning. It identifies the first action needed and executes. The results come back. The agent evaluates whether it's closer to the goal. It plans the next action. It executes again. This continues, perceive, reason, act until the goal is reached, an error condition is triggered, or the agent determines it cannot proceed and hands off to a human. What's important to notice is that workflow is the hand-off point. Good agent design always includes a point at which the agent recognizes the limits of its confidence and escalates. That's not a failure. It's responsible architecture. At Solara, an agent that flags an equipment anomaly it can't fully explain and routes it to a human engineer isn't falling short. It's doing exactly what it should.

scenes.voiceover_narration: Let's bring it together. Every agent is built from four components, perception, memory, reasoning, and action, working together in a continuous loop. That loop drives agent-environment interaction. The agent observes, decides, acts, and observes again. The three types of agents, reactive, goal-based, and utility-based, represent increasing levels of sophistication. Reactive agents are fast and rule-driven. Goal-based agents plan towards outcomes. Utility-based agents optimize across trade-offs. Coming up next, we're going hands-on. In the demo, we'll visualize types and architectures of AI agents in action, so you can see the decision loops and execution patterns we've been discussing actually running in real time. Let's take a look.
